title: MB8-03672
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX a citizen of Haiti, appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated January 12, 2018, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.

The determinative issues for the RPD were credibility and the risk to the Appellant. The RPD found that the Appellant was not credible with respect to the circumstances surrounding the land dispute and that there was no nexus to a Convention ground.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in: * its assessment of her credibility; * failing to establish a nexus to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) based on her the attempted rape in Haiti; * failing to accord probative value to the attempted rape and personal threats.
I do not find that the Appellant has established a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that she is a person in need of protection.
The appeal is denied.

The Appellant's Haitian residence is subject to a property dispute. The alleged facts are as follows. On XXXX XXXX, 2016, XXXX XXXX, accompanied by legal authorities, the police and bandits, ransacked and damaged her home and threatened her and her family with further violence if they did not vacate the land. Her cousin, XXXX XXXX XXXX, the legal landowner, was imprisoned. The Appellant fled to XXXX on a temporary basis before leaving to the United States on a valid visa to join her fiancé. She was married in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2016. On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the day after a marital rape, the Appellant left her husband, fled to Canada and requested asylum. ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION (RAD)

When reviewing the RPD decision, I am required to independently determine whether the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of law, fact or mixed fact and law. I may defer to the RPD's credibility assessment of oral testimony if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage in the circumstances.1 Reasons will be provided in my analysis if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage.2 I am applying a standard of correctness to this decision.
The determinative issues in this case are: * Fear based on being a woman and alleged rape in Haiti; * Credibility. Fear based on being a woman and alleged rape in Haiti
The Appellant argues that she suffers a serious possibility of persecution due to her membership as a woman in Haiti and considering that she was the victim of an attempted rape.
The RPD concluded that given the problems with her credibility, no link could be established between her individual case and a Convention ground.

I find that the RPD did not err in concluding that the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution or of a danger of torture or a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, should she be returned to Haiti, for the reasons that follow. The attempted rape in Haiti cannot be established on a balance of probabilities

Given the Appellant's credibility issues, the RPD did not find that there was nexus to a Convention ground. The Appellant argues that the very fact of the attempted rape establishes that nexus. I also find that the Appellant is not credible with respect to the attempted rape; therefore, there is no nexus. When the Appellant was asked why she was seeking protection, she stated that it was because bandits had invaded and ransacked her home. When asked if anything else had happened, she said no. When the member later asked her why she had not mentioned the attempted rape in her testimony, since it was in her Basis of Claim (BOC), she said that she was waiting to be asked the question. When it was explained to her that it was her responsibility to speak about the issue when asked an open-ended question, she responded, ok. Only when counsel asked her if there was anything else that she wanted to add did she mention the attempted rape. She did not mention any link between this incident and the bandits.

There is also the issue of when the attempted rape occurred. In her BOC, the Appellant states that the attempted rape occurred on the night that her cousin, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was arrested. As I explain in paragraph 19, the date of the arrest of XXXX XXXX XXXX is unclear. This lack of clarity causes me to believe that the claim of attempted rape is not credible.

Chairperson's Guidelines 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender Related Persecution state that victims of sexual violence can have trouble testifying to traumatic events. However, without being specifically prompted, the Appellant testified to being the victim of sexual violence at the hands of her American husband at the beginning of the hearing. While I offer the Appellant my sympathies for any traumas that she has experienced, I do not find it reasonable that the Appellant would spontaneously testify to one rape, while failing to raise another if it was an aspect of her experience that goes to the heart of her claim.

The documentary evidence does confirm that women in Haiti are subject to sexual violence3. While it is true that an attempted rape could be grounds for consideration under section 96, in this case, the Appellant is not credible with respect to the attempted rape. In light of the documentary evidence and considering that the Appellant's testimony is not credible, I find that the Appellant is not at risk as a woman, should she be returned to Haiti. The Appellant regularly returned home throughout the events of the land dispute

The RPD impugned the Appellant's credibility because she regularly returned to her home in Port-au-Prince despite the alleged danger to her. The Appellant presents no arguments to refute this finding. Though the Appellant left her home and went to XXXX, she testified to returning to the home under dispute every week in order to attend school. She slept in her primary home each week and returned to XXXX on the weekends. I find that if the Appellant truly feared persecution as a woman or a risk or threat for any other reason, she would not have stayed in her residence in Port-au-Prince. The Appellant fears the bandits in the context of the land dispute

In her BOC, the Appellant clearly states that she fears a return to Haiti because the bandits are still present and because she identified them to the police. She reiterated that fear during her testimony. I find that the Appellant's alleged fear is related to her residency in a home on disputed land and not because she is a woman in Haiti. Credibility
I find that the RPD did not err in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility for the reasons that follow. Confusion around the presence, absence and arrest of XXXX XXXX XXXX

The RPD further impugned the Appellant's credibility because her testimony regarding the presence or absence of XXXX XXXX XXXX was confusing. The Appellant argues that this issue is peripheral. I disagree. The circumstance surrounding the land dispute is determinative because it is the reason that the Appellant fears returning to Haiti. The Appellant was unable to convincingly testify to the arrest of her cousin, XXXX XXXX XXXX, as well as to his presence or absence in Haiti on the day of the first incident on XXXX XXXX, 2016. During her testimony, she testified that he was not at home at the time of the XXXX XXXX, 2016 incident and that he was in fact on vacation in XXXX. Later on, the Appellant testified that her cousin has been imprisoned since XXXX XXXX, 2016. When that contradiction was put to her, she said that she had confused the dates before concluding that her cousin was arrested on XXXX XXXX, 2016. In her BOC, the Appellant states that the arrest occurred following a police invasion on the date of the death of her cousin, XXXX XXXX XXXX. No date for the arrest is provided in her BOC. In her statement to the justice of the peace on XXXX XXXX, 2016, the Appellant states that the bandits returned to the house on XXXX XXXX, 2016 and that her cousin, XXXX XXXX XXXX, was imprisoned during that incident. If the arrest had happened on the date of her cousin's death, I find it reasonable that the Appellant would recall the incident with clarity. Since the arrest is central to the veracity of the land dispute, the fact that the Appellant cannot with certainty confirm the presence of the principal landowner at home and cannot confirm the dates of his arrests detracts significantly from her credibility. Omission of death threats in her BOC and in the written statement of the justice of the peace

The RPD impugned the Appellant's credibility because, after testifying to receiving death threats, she did not satisfactorily explain why she omitted them in her BOC. In her memorandum, the Appellant maintains that she did provide a reasonable response and that the negative credibility finding does not discount her need for protection. Again, I disagree. I do not find that the Appellant has established that there were death threats on a balance of probabilities and therefore, she does not need protection.

The Appellant testified to receiving death threats on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and that this was the reason that she went to see a justice of the peace. However, in the justice of the peace's written report, the threats are not mentioned. In her BOC and in the justice of the peace's report, the Appellant describes a home invasion leading to the arrest of her cousin and precipitating the death of another cousin. These events are alleged to occur on XXXX XXXX, 2018. It is only during testimony that the death threats are mentioned. When confronted with the absence of the death threats in the documentary evidence, the Appellant reiterated that the XXXX XXXX, 2016 death threats were the reason that she went to the justice of the peace. I do not find it reasonable that someone fearing for their life would not raise the death threats before the justice of the peace and indicate them in the BOC, which explicitly asks about the nature of any threats. I find that this omission detracts significantly from her credibility. The absence of ongoing threats

In its closing comments, the RPD mentioned that the Appellant has not received any personal threats since leaving Haiti and thus, was not in danger, should she be returned to her country of origin. The Appellant argues that the absence of ongoing threats does not discount the need for protection. I disagree. Forward-facing risk is a key component of evaluating the Appellant's need for protection. As I have already found that the Appellant is not credible with respect to the risk that she faces as a result of the land dispute, I will not address this issue.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
